texts: good. the day-111 / Year-1 date and the past marking attach directly to Lantern-night itself, which is how an event-denoting name carries its own occurrence; nothing in the sentence is dropped or over-stated.

good. the superlative is recorded (Lantern-night as the longest of the nights) together with Lantern-night being a night. Two limits no rewording fixes, so don't churn this sentence: a superlative has no slot for a restricting domain, so "of the year" is not separately recorded (nothing false is asserted either way), and because Lantern-night is a name, this timeless claim and the previous sentence's day-111 occurrence land on one and the same symbol, so the recurring festival and that year's instance are not told apart.
good. "the night" resolves back to Lantern-night, and clear, cold and the "very" degree are each recorded as past states of it.

good. parses as a rule that can actually fire — every lantern in Aelmere gets its own past lighting, with the in-Aelmere restriction sitting in the rule's condition where a lantern named later can match it.

mixed: the lighting, the sundown time, the Stilllight Lantern and Meren's office as speaker of the Council are all recorded, but nothing ties the office to the act — an in-what-capacity "as"-phrase has no carrier, so "in what capacity did he light it?" cannot be answered. If that link matters, split it into two clauses joined by a connective: "Meren Tallowhand was the speaker of the Council, so Meren Tallowhand lit the Stilllight Lantern at sundown." The cost is that the office then reads as the reason for the act rather than only the capacity.
good. one past walking event per villager, carrying the Cliff Path, midnight, the harbor-wall start and the cliff-spire end, and the rule fires for any villager named later.
good. the wind and its coldness, the manner "strongly", and "that night" resolved onto day 111 of Year 1 are all recorded.
good. a rule that can fire — every lantern on the Cliff Path gets its own past holding, with the on-the-path restriction in the condition.
good. the past walking, Coraline Ash as the walker and "beside Pell" are all recorded.
good. same shape as the previous sentence — the past walking, Joren Salt as the walker, and "beside Meren Tallowhand".

mixed: the harbor fires, "until dawn" and a telling for each villager all land, but "stories" is stored as the bare kind rather than as a set of stories that actually got told, so nothing can later point back at them ("one of those stories …"). Give the object a determiner or a count so the stories get their own referent: "The villagers told their stories at the harbor fires until dawn." The only cost is the added shade that the stories are theirs; "several stories" works the same way if you would rather add a vague count.

mixed: Old Vesh, the telling, the story and the bad winter (correctly dated sixty-three years back) are each recorded, but the "of"-phrase joining them is dropped entirely — nothing says what the story was about, which is the point of the sentence. Use "about", which does have a carrier: "Old Vesh told the story about the bad winter of sixty-three years ago."

good. the three sky-cats, the cliff-spires (the same ones as in the Cliff Path sentence), the morning and the past all land, with the visibility given to each cat separately rather than asserted of the trio as an object.
